content: Tetanus is a medical condition characterized by prolonged contraction of skeletal muscle fibers. The primary symptoms are caused by tetanospasmin, a neurotoxin produced by the Gram-positive, obligate anaerobic bacterium Clostridium tetani. Infection typically occurs through wound contamination, often involving cuts or deep puncture wounds. As the infection progresses, muscle spasms in the jaw develop, leading to the common name lockjaw. This is followed by difficulty swallowing, generalized muscle stiffness, and spasms in other parts of the body. Proper immunization and post-exposure prophylaxis can prevent infection. Tetanus primarily affects skeletal muscle, a type of striated muscle. However, cardiac muscle, another type of striated muscle, cannot be tetanized due to its intrinsic electrical properties. In recent years, approximately 11% of reported tetanus cases have been fatal, with the highest mortality rates observed in unvaccinated individuals and those over 60 years of age. Clostridium tetani, the bacterium responsible for tetanus, is recovered from the initial wound in only about 30% of cases and can also be found in individuals without tetanus. The clinical manifestations of tetanus occur when the tetanus toxin blocks inhibitory nerve impulses by interfering with neurotransmitter release, leading to unopposed muscle contraction and spasms. Seizures may occur, and the autonomic nervous system can also be affected. The term tetany refers to sustained muscle contraction not caused by tetanus. In 1884, Carle and Rattone discovered tetanus by injecting animals with pus from a patient who had died of the disease. In 1924, Descombey developed the tetanus toxoid, which was extensively used during World War II. Tetanus can be classified into neonatal, cephalic, generalized, or localized forms based on its patterns of presentation. The bacterium Clostridium tetani is introduced into the human body, usually through a wound. The toxins produced by the bacterium utilize the blood and/or lymphatic system to access target tissues. These toxins can act at various sites in the central nervous system, including the spinal cord, peripheral motor end plates, and the brain. They can also affect the sympathetic nervous system. Clostridium tetani is a rod-shaped, anaerobic bacterium of the genus Clostridium. Like other Clostridium species, it is Gram-positive, and its appearance on a Gram stain resembles tennis rackets or drumsticks. C. tetani is found as spores in soil or as parasites in the gastrointestinal tract of animals. It produces a potent biological toxin, tetanospasmin, which is the causative agent of tetanus. Tetanus must be differentiated from other conditions such as strychnine poisoning, dental infections, drug reactions, hypocalcemia, meningitis, stroke, and stiff person syndrome. Tetanus is an infectious disease that is not contagious and can be prevented with a vaccine. In the United States, there are fewer than 100 cases of tetanus annually, with around five deaths attributed to the disease each year. Globally, approximately one million cases of tetanus are reported annually, leading to an estimated 300,000 to 500,000 deaths. The incidence of tetanus is higher in individuals over 65 years of age and is more commonly seen in Hispanic populations. Clostridium tetani spores can be found in various locations, including manure, soil, and dust. People living in developing countries are at higher risk of acquiring tetanus due to a lack of vaccination and less emphasis on general hygiene. Risk factors for tetanus include contaminated wounds, puncture wounds, crushing injuries, burns, and working in unhygienic environments. The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) has not recommended any specific guidelines for tetanus screening. The incubation period for tetanus ranges from 2 to 38 days, with a median of 7 days post-exposure. The presentation and progression of the disease may vary depending on the type of tetanus. Generalized tetanus can involve the respiratory muscles, making breathing difficult. Complications of tetanus include fractures, laryngospasm, aspiration pneumonia, and pulmonary embolism. The fatality rate of tetanus is approximately 11%, with prolonged convulsions and contractions contributing to mortality. Tetanus without spasms has an excellent prognosis, and early diagnosis is associated with a favorable outcome. The history of a patient presenting with tetanus typically reveals contamination of an injury or wound with soil, rust-containing metal, or manure. Puncture wounds, burns, animal scratches, fractures, otitis media, and contaminated surgical wounds (e.g., gastrointestinal surgeries or abortions) are common sources. A history of recent accidents or injuries in contaminated environments is helpful in making a diagnosis. Key symptoms include trismus (lockjaw), spasms of the facial muscles (risus sardonicus), neck stiffness, and difficulty swallowing. Tetanus is primarily a clinical diagnosis, as there are no specific laboratory findings characteristic of the disease. Diagnosis is based on a detailed history and thorough physical examination. Bacteriologic confirmation is not required, as C. tetani can be found in individuals without tetanus, and only 30% of tetanic wounds may yield the pathogen. Imaging studies such as X-rays, CT scans, MRIs, and ultrasounds do not provide diagnostic findings for tetanus. Tetanus is a medical emergency requiring immediate treatment. Medical therapy includes hospitalization, administration of human tetanus immune globulin (TIG) or equine antitoxin (if human immune globulin is unavailable), a tetanus toxoid booster, agents to control muscle spasms, aggressive wound care, and antimicrobial therapy. Mechanical ventilation and agents to manage autonomic nervous system instability may be necessary for severe cases. The only surgical intervention required for tetanus management is wound debridement, which involves cleaning the contaminated wound. Primary prevention of tetanus involves vaccination against Clostridium tetani. Other preventive measures include proper wound care, avoiding injuries, wearing protective equipment, maintaining clean surroundings, controlling diabetes, ensuring aseptic gynecological procedures, managing burn and compound fracture injuries aggressively, and avoiding intravenous drug abuse. Secondary prevention includes post-exposure care for individuals with uncertain vaccination history or incomplete primary vaccination. These patients typically receive passive immunity with tetanus immune globulin (TIG). The primary cost associated with tetanus is the vaccine itself, which is available under various trade names with slightly different costs. Vaccines are categorized into pediatric and adult doses. The DTaP vaccine, mentioned in the context of tetanus prevention, stands for Diphtheria, Tetanus, and Pertussis.
